'''David Edward Pritchard''' (born October 15, 1941)<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?pritchardd |title=Biography on APS |access-date=2012-07-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307022423/https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?pritchardd |archive-date=2016-03-07 |url-status=dead }}</ref> is a professor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) who specializes in [[atomic physics]] and [[educational research]].

== Career ==

=== Early work ===
Pritchard completed his PhD in 1968 at [[Harvard University]] under the supervision of [[Daniel Kleppner]]. His thesis involved building the first atomic scattering machine with polarized atoms to study differential [[Spin-exchange|spin exchange]] scattering, a process by which the [[Hydrogen line|21 cm hydrogen line]] manifests.<ref name="thesis"/>

Pritchard was an early adopter of [[tunable laser]]s in physics and chemistry, demonstrating high-resolution [[spectroscopy]] through the simultaneous absorption of two laser photons. He employed both laser and radio-frequency spectroscopy to study weakly bound [[van der Waals molecule]]s, such as NaNe<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ahmad-Bitar |first1=Riad |last2=Lapatovich |first2=Walter P. |last3=Pritchard |first3=David E. |last4=Renhorn |first4=Ingemar |date=1977-12-26 |title=Laser Spectroscopy of Bound NaNe Molecules |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.39.1657 |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=39 |issue=26 |pages=1657–1660 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.39.1657 |bibcode=1977PhRvL..39.1657A |issn=0031-9007|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and KAr,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mattison |first1=Edward M. |last2=Pritchard |first2=David E. |last3=Kleppner |first3=Daniel |date=1974-03-11 |title=Spin-Rotation Coupling in the Alkali---Rare-Gas Van der Waals Molecule KAr |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.32.507 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=32 |issue=10 |pages=507–509 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.32.507|bibcode=1974PhRvL..32..507M |url-access=subscription }}</ref> in cold supersonic [[molecular beam]]s.

=== Atom optics, atom traps, and atom interferometers ===
Pritchard made use of tunable lasers' ability to transfer [[momentum]] to atoms, leading to demonstrations of the [[diffraction]] of atoms from a standing wave of light (denoted [[Kapitsa–Dirac effect|Kapitza-Dirac]] or Raman-Nath regimes) and [[Bragg's law|Bragg scattering]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Martin |first1=Peter J. |last2=Oldaker |first2=Bruce G. |last3=Miklich |first3=Andrew H. |last4=Pritchard |first4=David E. |date=1988-02-08 |title=Bragg scattering of atoms from a standing light wave |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.60.515 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=60 |issue=6 |pages=515–518 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.60.515|pmid=10038570 |bibcode=1988PhRvL..60..515M |url-access=subscription }}</ref> of atoms from [[Diffraction grating|light gratings]], founding the field of coherent [[atom optics]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wieman |first1=Carl E. |last2=Pritchard |first2=David E. |last3=Wineland |first3=David J. |date=1999-03-01 |title=Atom cooling, trapping, and quantum manipulation |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/RevModPhys.71.S253 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=71 |issue=2 |pages=S253–S262 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.71.S253|bibcode=1999RvMPS..71..253W |url-access=subscription }}</ref>  This led to the creation of the first [[atom interferometer]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Keith |first1=David W. |last2=Ekstrom |first2=Christopher R. |last3=Turchette |first3=Quentin A. |last4=Pritchard |first4=David E. |date=1991-05-27 |title=An interferometer for atoms |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1103/physrevlett.66.2693 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=66 |issue=21 |pages=2693–2696 |doi=10.1103/physrevlett.66.2693 |pmid=10043592 |bibcode=1991PhRvL..66.2693K |issn=0031-9007|url-access=subscription }}</ref> where [[matter waves]] would propagate on both sides of a metal foil before recombining, so that different interactions on the two sides would result in a [[fringe shift]] of the atomic interference pattern.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ekstrom |first1=Christopher R. |last2=Schmiedmayer |first2=Jörg |last3=Chapman |first3=Michael S. |last4=Hammond |first4=Troy D. |last5=Pritchard |first5=David E. |date=1995-05-01 |title=Measurement of the electric polarizability of sodium with an atom interferometer |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1103/physreva.51.3883 |journal=Physical Review A |volume=51 |issue=5 |pages=3883–3888 |doi=10.1103/physreva.51.3883 |pmid=9912059 |bibcode=1995PhRvA..51.3883E |issn=1050-2947|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This allowed for precise measurements of atomic [[polarizability]], the [[refractive index]] of gaseous matter waves, and fundamental testing of [[quantum decoherence]], as well as the first demonstration of the ability of atom interferometers to measure angular velocity like a [[gyroscope]] and to work for complex particles like Na<sub>2</sub> molecules in the gaseous phase.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cronin |first1=Alexander D. |last2=Schmiedmayer |first2=Jörg |last3=Pritchard |first3=David E. |date=2009-07-28 |title=Optics and interferometry with atoms and molecules |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1103/revmodphys.81.1051 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=81 |issue=3 |pages=1051–1129 |doi=10.1103/revmodphys.81.1051 |arxiv=0712.3703 |bibcode=2009RvMP...81.1051C |issn=0034-6861|hdl=1721.1/52372 |s2cid=28009912 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

A singularly important development from atom optics is Pritchard's invention of the [[magneto-optical trap]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pritchard |first1=D. E. |last2=Raab |first2=E. L. |last3=Bagnato |first3=V. |last4=Wieman |first4=C. E. |last5=Watts |first5=R. N. |date=1986-07-21 |title=Light Traps Using Spontaneous Forces |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1103/physrevlett.57.310 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=57 |issue=3 |pages=310–313 |doi=10.1103/physrevlett.57.310 |pmid=10034027 |bibcode=1986PhRvL..57..310P |s2cid=42773639 |issn=0031-9007|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which captures and cools atoms to sub-millikelvin temperatures and of the Dark SPOT MOT, in which atoms are confined in a way such that they do not interact with trapping light.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ketterle |first1=Wolfgang |last2=Davis |first2=Kendall B. |last3=Joffe |first3=Michael A. |last4=Martin |first4=Alex |last5=Pritchard |first5=David E. |date=1993-04-12 |title=High densities of cold atoms in a''dark''spontaneous-force optical trap |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1103/physrevlett.70.2253 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=70 |issue=15 |pages=2253–2256 |doi=10.1103/physrevlett.70.2253 |pmid=10053514 |bibcode=1993PhRvL..70.2253K |issn=0031-9007|url-access=subscription |hdl=10261/246886 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Together with a [[Magnetic trap (atoms)|magnetic atom trap]], it can compress ~ 10<sup>10</sup> cold atoms into the same small volume (This is sometimes called the [[Ioffe-Pritchard trap]] to honor its plasma physics origin). These traps are commonly used in the field of cold atom research and are the foundational tools for the MIT-Harvard Center for [[Ultracold atom|Ultracold Atoms]]''.''

In 1990, Pritchard brought [[Wolfgang Ketterle]] to [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] as a [[postdoctoral research]]er to work on [[Laser cooling|atom cooling]]. To encourage Ketterle to stay at MIT, in 1993 Ketterle was given his own experimental cold atom program (with two students and two grants) while Pritchard himself stepped aside from the field to allow Ketterle to be appointed to the faculty. Ketterle pursued atom cooling to achieve [[Bose–Einstein condensation]] in 1995, a discovery for which Ketterle was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] in 2001, alongside Pritchard's former graduate student, [[Eric Allin Cornell]], and [[Carl Wieman]], who was an informal Pritchard mentee while an undergraduate at MIT.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 2001 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2001/summary/ |access-date=2024-02-03 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref>

Ketterle and Pritchard then partnered to study atom optics and interferometry with Bose condensates, demonstrating coherent amplification of [[matter wave]]s, [[Superradiance|superradiant]] [[Rayleigh scattering]], and the power of Bragg spectroscopy to probe the condensate and used laser light to establish coherence between two condensates that never touch. Pritchard received the 2004 [[Max Born Award]], "For creative application of light to new forms of spectroscopy, to manipulation and trapping of atoms, and for pioneering the new fields of atom optics and atom interferometry".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2004-06-02 |title=Awards and Honors |url=https://news.mit.edu/2004/aandh-0602 |access-date=2024-09-18 |website=MIT News {{!}} Massachusetts Institute of Technology |language=en}}</ref>

=== Precise measurements of atomic masses ===
Pritchard is a pioneer in the precise measurement of atomic and molecular masses using [[ion trap]]s, an advance enabled by his group's developing highly sensitive radio-frequency detectors based on [[SQUID]]s  (superconducting quantum interference devices) and techniques to coherently cross-couple the motion of different modes of an ion's oscillation in the trap.  These advances culminated in an ion balance in which one each of two different ions were simultaneously confined while their [[Cyclotron motion#Cyclotron resonance|cyclotron frequencies]] were inter-compared to better than one part in 10<sup>11</sup>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rainville |first1=Simon |last2=Thompson |first2=James K. |last3=Pritchard |first3=David E. |date=2004-01-16 |title=An Ion Balance for Ultra-High-Precision Atomic Mass Measurements |journal=Science |volume=303 |issue=5656 |pages=334–338 |doi=10.1126/science.1092320 |pmid=14671311 |bibcode=2004Sci...303..334R |s2cid=10927619 |issn=0036-8075|doi-access=free }}</ref>  This led to the discovery of a new type of systematic shift of the cyclotron frequency due to the polarizability of the ion, providing the most accurate measurement of ionic molecule polarizability.  It also resulted in a fifty-fold improvement of experimental tests of [[Albert Einstein]]'s [[mass–energy equivalence]] that <math>E=mc^2</math> (where ''E'' is the energy, ''m'' is the mass and ''c'' the [[speed of light]]) – now at ½ part per million.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rainville |first1=Simon |last2=Thompson |first2=James K. |last3=Myers |first3=Edmund G. |last4=Brown |first4=John M. |last5=Dewey |first5=Maynard S. |last6=Kessler |first6=Ernest G. |last7=Deslattes |first7=Richard D. |last8=Börner |first8=Hans G. |last9=Jentschel |first9=Michael |last10=Mutti |first10=Paolo |last11=Pritchard |first11=David E. |date=2005 |title=A direct test of E=mc2 |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/4381096a |journal=Nature |volume=438 |issue=7071 |pages=1096–1097 |doi=10.1038/4381096a |pmid=16371997 |s2cid=4426118 |issn=0028-0836|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Precise measurements of the masses of [[rubidium]] and [[caesium]] atoms made with the MIT apparatus have been combined with others' high-precision atom interferometric measurements of ''h''/''m'' (the [[Planck constant]] divided by the atom mass) to give the most accurate value of the fine structure constant at 0.2&nbsp;ppb (parts per billion), differing by ~ 2.5 combined errors from measurement based on [[quantum electrodynamics]]. This is the most precise comparison of measurements made using entirely different theoretical bases.

== Teaching and education software ==
In 1998, David Pritchard and his son Alex developed an online Socratic tutor, mycybertutor.com, which provides specific critiques of incorrect symbolic answers, hints upon request, and follow-up comments and questions. This tool has been shown to significantly improve students' ability to answer traditional MIT examination problems, increasing their performance by approximately 2 standard deviations.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Morote |first1=Elsa-Sofia |last2=Pritchard |first2=David E. |date=2009-08-01 |title=What course elements correlate with improvement on tests in introductory Newtonian mechanics? |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1119/1.3139533 |journal=American Journal of Physics |volume=77 |issue=8 |pages=746–753 |doi=10.1119/1.3139533 |bibcode=2009AmJPh..77..746M |issn=0002-9505|hdl=1721.1/51717 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The software is now marketed as Mastering Physics, Mastering Chemistry, and Mastering Astronomy by [[Pearson Education]]. It has become a widely used homework tutor in Science and Engineering, with approximately 2.5 million.

Pritchard's education research group, RELATE<ref>{{Cite web |title=Relate {{!}} Research in Learning, Assessing and Tutoring Effectively |url=https://www.rle.mit.edu/relate/ |access-date=2023-08-03 |language=en-US}}</ref> was started in 2000 with the goal to "Apply the principles and techniques of science and engineering to study and improve learning, especially of expertise''"''.  They conduct research using all components in the acronym RELATE - Research in Learning, Assessing, and Tutoring Effectively.   They showed that copying online homework is by far the best predictor of a low final exam grade in MIT residential physics,<ref name=":0" /> and is the dominant contributor to ~ 5% of the certificates given by [[edX]]. They explored new types of instruction (e.g. deliberate practice of critical problem-solving skills) or variations in instruction (adding a diagram, replacing multiple choice questions with more interactive drag and drop questions, etc.) compared with traditional instruction (the control).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Zhongzhou |last2=Chudzicki |first2=Christopher |last3=Palumbo |first3=Daniel |last4=Alexandron |first4=Giora |last5=Choi |first5=Youn-Jeng |last6=Zhou |first6=Qian |last7=Pritchard |first7=David E. |date=2016 |title=Researching for better instructional methods using AB experiments in MOOCs: results and challenges |journal=Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning |language=en |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=9 |doi=10.1186/s41039-016-0034-4 |issn=1793-7078 |pmc=6302917 |pmid=30613242 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Chudzicki |first1=Christopher |last2=Pritchard |first2=David E. |last3=Chen |first3=Zhongzhou |title=Proceedings of the Second (2015) ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale |chapter=Learning Experiments Using AB Testing at Scale |date=2015-03-14 |pages=405–408 |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1145/2724660.2728703 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=ACM |doi=10.1145/2724660.2728703|hdl=1721.1/99202 |isbn=9781450334112 |s2cid=42124185 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

These experiments, along with other relevant research, indicated an important principle that students were struggling with – strategic thinking – the ability to determine which concepts and procedures are helpful in solving an unfamiliar problem.  For this purpose, RELATE developed a Mechanics Reasoning Inventory<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pawl |first1=Andrew |last2=Barrantes |first2=Analia |last3=Cardamone |first3=Carolin |last4=Rayyan |first4=Saif |last5=Pritchard |first5=David E. |last6=Rebello |first6=N. Sanjay |last7=Engelhardt |first7=Paula V. |last8=Singh |first8=Chandralekha |date=2012 |title=Development of a mechanics reasoning inventory |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.3680051 |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |volume=1413 |issue=1 |pages=287–290 |publisher=AIP |doi=10.1063/1.3680051|bibcode=2012AIPC.1413..287P |hdl=1721.1/78556 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> that measures strategic ability; it served as a benchmark of progress for their new pedagogy: Modeling Approach to Problem-Solving.  This pedagogy was shown to greatly improve students' attitudes towards learning science, raise their scores on the Physics 1 final exam retake,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pawl |first1=Andrew |last2=Barrantes |first2=Analia |last3=Pritchard |first3=David E. |last4=Sabella |first4=Mel |last5=Henderson |first5=Charles |last6=Singh |first6=Chandralekha |date=2009 |title=Modeling Applied to Problem Solving |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.3266752 |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |volume=1179 |issue=1 |pages=51–54 |publisher=AIP |doi=10.1063/1.3266752|bibcode=2009AIPC.1179...51P |hdl=1721.1/76354 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and subsequently help them improve their Physics 2 grade by ~&nbsp;{{sfrac|1|2}} standard deviation relative to students who didn't benefit from this intervention.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rayyan |first1=Saif |last2=Pawl |first2=Andrew |last3=Barrantes |first3=Analia |last4=Teodorescu |first4=Raluca |last5=Pritchard |first5=David E. |last6=Singh |first6=Chandralekha |last7=Sabella |first7=Mel |last8=Rebello |first8=Sanjay |date=2010 |title=Improved Student Performance In Electricity And Magnetism Following Prior MAPS Instruction In Mechanics |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.3515221 |journal=AIP Conference Proceedings |volume=1289 |issue=1 |pages=273–276 |publisher=AIP |doi=10.1063/1.3515221|bibcode=2010AIPC.1289..273R |hdl=1721.1/63094 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
